paragraphs: Matching short texts involves deciding whether two pieces of language fit together, such as a question and a relevant answer. A common approach maps each object into a feature space and measures the match through an inner product. The paper argues that this arrangement can miss richer relationships involved in matching complicated objects.

The authors propose a deep architecture designed to represent those relationships more effectively. Its central organizing ideas are locality and hierarchy in natural language: matching involves structure at different levels, rather than only a single comparison between overall representations. The architecture brings these properties together when comparing objects from different domains or roles.

The paper applies the approach to language tasks, including finding sensible tweet responses and relevant answers to questions. It reports substantial improvements over the state-of-the-art models. The contribution is therefore an architecture that gives the matching process itself more expressive structure, with reported benefits for the natural-language tasks considered.
neurips-2013-a-deep-architecture-for-mat.tldr: A deep architecture uses locality and hierarchy in language to improve matching between short texts.

paragraphs: People contributing data may want different amounts of privacy. This paper formalizes an adaptive anonymity problem in which each person supplies both their data and an integer expressing their desired anonymity level. The privacy requirement therefore becomes part of the input for each individual, rather than a single setting imposed uniformly on everyone.

The authors generalize k-anonymity into a formulation based on b-matching and develop algorithms and theory for implementing it. The central change is that the formulation accommodates different anonymity requirements within the same problem. This makes individual preferences a direct part of how the anonymization task is defined and solved.

The abstract reports that the relaxation improves utility while retaining theoretical privacy guarantees of equal strength within the comparison being made. Experiments on benchmark and social datasets also show improved utility. The stated result is that allowing personal anonymity levels can preserve more useful information while providing the formal protections established for this framework.
neurips-2013-adaptive-anonymity-via-b-ma.tldr: A b-matching formulation supports individual anonymity preferences while improving data utility and retaining strong theoretical privacy guarantees.

paragraphs: Many graph-based learning methods assign values to vertices using information from their neighbors. This paper identifies a shared harmonic structure across several familiar models: a vertex's value is approximately a weighted average of nearby values. Making that shared structure explicit gives the authors a common way to study methods that otherwise appear different.

The analysis connects variation across a graph cut with harmonic loss and cut cost. The authors derive both upper and lower bounds using the ratio of these quantities. These bounds link the behavior of the learned values to the graph's connectivity and to how closely the target function follows its harmonic structure.

The resulting analytical tool covers absorbing and partially absorbing random walks, hitting times, the graph Laplacian's pseudoinverse, and Laplacian eigenvectors. The authors report that it explains several previously open questions about these models and supplies theoretical guidance for their use. Simulations on synthetic and real datasets support the analysis.
neurips-2013-analyzing-the-harmonic-stru.tldr: A shared harmonic structure yields bounds that explain the behavior of five established graph-learning models.

paragraphs: Monte-Carlo tree search supports planning under uncertainty, including situations with little domain knowledge. A central challenge is deciding how much effort to spend investigating uncertain actions versus pursuing actions that already look promising. This paper introduces a Bayesian approach to that exploration and exploitation trade-off.

The proposed DNG-MCTS algorithm represents uncertainty about an action's accumulated reward using a mixture of Normal distributions. Bayesian inference uses conjugate priors combining Dirichlet and NormalGamma distributions. This construction gives the algorithm a structured representation of reward uncertainty, which is then used by Thompson sampling to select actions at decision nodes in the search tree.

The authors evaluate the algorithm for online planning in general Markov decision processes and report state-of-the-art performance in comparisons with the popular UCT algorithm. The result supports using richer reward-uncertainty models to guide search. Its reported advantage is empirical: the abstract establishes the approach through the planning experiments rather than asserting that it always selects better actions.
neurips-2013-bayesian-mixture-modelling-.tldr: DNG-MCTS combines Bayesian reward mixtures with Thompson sampling to guide exploration and exploitation in tree search.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning often needs a compact representation of a value function, and the choice of features affects the quality of that approximation. This paper addresses how to generate useful features automatically. It builds on Bellman Error Basis Functions, which use the current approximation's error to guide the construction of additional features.

Earlier results established that these basis functions can improve policy-evaluation error at a rate comparable to value iteration. The authors propose a simple algorithm that generates them through random projections in sparse feature spaces. The aim is to make error-directed feature generation fast and robust when the original representation has many dimensions but relatively few active features.

The paper provides a finite-sample analysis and proves that projections with dimension logarithmic in the original space's dimension guarantee error contraction in the analyzed setting. Experiments demonstrate the method's strength in domains where choosing a good state representation is difficult. Together, these results connect compact randomized representations with theoretically supported improvements in value approximation.
neurips-2013-bellman-error-based-feature.tldr: Random projections efficiently generate Bellman-error features for sparse representations, with finite-sample guarantees of error contraction.

paragraphs: Correlated Nystrom Views, or XNV, is a semi-supervised method for regression and classification. It combines inexpensive random features with information from unlabeled examples. The algorithm first generates two feature views, then uses canonical correlation analysis on unlabeled data to steer regression toward useful features.

The motivation comes from a conditional result about multiview regression: when the views contain accurate estimators, this procedure can substantially reduce variance while adding little bias. The paper connects that requirement to existing theoretical and empirical findings that random-feature regression closely approximates kernel regression. This provides a rationale for constructing the two views cheaply rather than requiring elaborate representations.

Across a wide variety of real-world datasets, the authors report that XNV consistently outperforms a state-of-the-art semi-supervised algorithm. They find better predictions, less variability in performance, and runtime reductions of orders of magnitude. These findings suggest that inexpensive feature construction and correlation information from unlabeled data can work together effectively in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2013-correlated-random-features-.tldr: XNV uses correlated random-feature views and unlabeled data to improve semi-supervised prediction while greatly reducing runtime.

paragraphs: Clustering distributed data requires attention to both the quality of the resulting groups and the communication needed to compute them. This paper develops algorithms for two standard center-based clustering objectives, k-means and k-median. Its focus is reducing communication while retaining provable guarantees about the clustering approach.

The method follows a coreset strategy: replace the full clustering problem with a small summary that supports finding a low-cost clustering. The main contribution is a distributed procedure for constructing a global coreset. By organizing the computation around this smaller representation, the algorithms reduce communication complexity compared with previous methods.

The construction works across general communication topologies, making the network structure an explicit part of the distributed setting. The paper also supplies experiments on synthetic and real datasets as evidence for the approach. Its significance lies in combining a compact global representation, lower communication requirements, and theoretical guarantees, rather than treating distributed clustering purely as a matter of splitting computation among machines.
neurips-2013-distributed-k-means-and-k-m.tldr: Distributed coreset construction reduces communication for k-means and k-median clustering across general network topologies.

paragraphs: Many learning methods need a manageable subset that represents a much larger dataset. The selection problem can often be expressed as maximizing a submodular set function while limiting the number of chosen elements. Classical approaches assume access to all the data in one place, which can be impractical at very large scales.

The paper introduces GreeDI, a simple two-stage distributed protocol that fits MapReduce-style computation. It addresses representative selection while the data are distributed, allowing the computation to be organized without relying on the centralized access required by classical approaches. The authors also provide a theoretical analysis of the protocol's performance.

That analysis shows that performance close to the centralized approach can be achieved under certain natural conditions; it is not an unconditional equivalence. Extensive experiments demonstrate effectiveness across several applications. These include sparse Gaussian process inference using Hadoop on tens of millions of examples, showing the method's relevance to representative selection at substantial data scales.
neurips-2013-distributed-submodular-maxi.tldr: GreeDI distributes representative-subset selection and can approach centralized performance under stated conditions.

paragraphs: A search engine must choose which advertisements to display while learning which choices are most profitable. Since feedback is only partial, this can be formulated as a stochastic multi-armed bandit problem. The paper examines what happens when standard bandit algorithms are applied naively to this advertising setting.

The authors identify two kinds of estimation bias with different consequences. Sample selection bias reduces the search engine's expected revenue. A second effect, called estimation-of-the-largest-mean bias, increases advertisers' game-theoretic player-regret. The distinction matters because the selection system affects both the platform choosing advertisements and the advertisers participating in it.

The paper then proposes simple corrections for these biases and reports benefits for both sides. Its contribution is to connect statistical estimation problems in adaptive advertisement selection with economic consequences for the participants. This means that judging the selection procedure involves more than whether it learns profitable ads: the biases can also change the quality of outcomes experienced by advertisers.
neurips-2013-estimation-bias-in-multi-ar.tldr: Naive bandit-based ad selection creates two harmful estimation biases, motivating corrections that benefit search engines and advertisers.

paragraphs: Sparse principal subspace estimation seeks dominant directions of variation with a sparse structure. This paper replaces the original estimation problem with a convex relaxation based on the Fantope, the convex hull of rank-d projection matrices. The resulting optimization problem can be solved efficiently using the alternating direction method of multipliers.

The authors establish a near-optimal statistical convergence rate expressed through sparsity, ambient dimension, and sample size. Their analysis applies to a general covariance matrix without requiring the spiked covariance model. For a one-dimensional target subspace, the result also establishes near-optimality of DSPCA even when the optimization solution itself is not rank one.

The paper additionally develops a framework for analyzing the method with arbitrary input matrices. This extends the settings in which statistical guarantees can be obtained beyond the initial covariance formulation. An application involving Kendall's tau correlation matrices and transelliptical component analysis illustrates that broader reach, linking an efficiently solvable relaxation to flexible statistical estimation.
neurips-2013-fantope-projection-and-sele.tldr: A Fantope-based convex relaxation efficiently estimates sparse principal subspaces with near-optimal statistical guarantees.

paragraphs: Many object detectors spend substantial computation applying linear templates to candidate feature windows. This paper targets that operation directly, aiming to accelerate the full recognition system rather than only an isolated calculation. The proposed method approximates template scores by vector-quantizing feature windows and combines this with additional acceleration techniques, including a cascade.

The procedure exposes two ways to balance speed and accuracy. One is choosing the number of vector-quantization levels, which controls the representation used for approximate scoring. The other is deciding whether to rescore windows. These choices allow the same basic method to support different computational and accuracy requirements.

The authors state that the method can be plugged into recognition systems using linear templates. Their demonstrations speed up the original Exemplar SVM detector by one order of magnitude and Deformable Part models by two, without accuracy loss in those evaluations. The reported findings show that approximate intermediate scoring can deliver substantial end-to-end acceleration while preserving final detection accuracy.
neurips-2013-fast-template-evaluation-wi.tldr: Vector-quantized template scoring substantially accelerates two object detectors without accuracy loss in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Structured prediction produces labels whose parts must be considered together. This paper develops efficient learning methods for randomized maximum-a-posteriori predictors, addressing non-decomposable loss functions. Its approach constructs posterior distributions over perturbations and adjusts those distributions using stochastic gradient methods.

A central theoretical result is that every smooth posterior distribution suffices to define a smooth PAC-Bayesian risk bound suitable for gradient optimization. This provides a connection between the randomization used by a predictor and an objective that can be optimized during learning. The authors also examine how choosing the posterior affects the computational properties of MAP prediction.

Two constructions make that connection concrete. Multiplicative posteriors are proposed for learning super-modular potentials compatible with specialized predictors such as graph cuts. Label-augmented posterior models can instead use efficient MAP approximations, including linear-program relaxations. The contribution therefore joins statistical learning criteria with computational structure, so posterior design can support both trainability and efficient structured prediction.
neurips-2013-learning-efficient-random-m.tldr: Smooth perturbation posteriors enable gradient-based learning of randomized structured predictors while accommodating efficient MAP algorithms.

paragraphs: Matrix completion attempts to reconstruct a matrix from only some of its entries. A standard strategy chooses the lowest-complexity matrix consistent with the observations, measuring complexity through rank or trace norm. Many guarantees for this strategy assume that observed entries were sampled randomly, an assumption that often does not hold in practice.

The paper retains that reconstruction step but changes how its output is assessed. After finding a consistent low-complexity matrix, the method finds a probability distribution over unobserved entries. It then proves a generalization-error bound with respect to that distribution, allowing guarantees to be obtained for any initial observation set.

The distribution is essential to interpreting the result: the guarantee concerns error under the constructed weighting of missing entries, rather than automatically providing uniform accuracy everywhere. The bound improves as the observed set becomes more complex according to the paper's specified measure. This offers a way to extract meaningful performance guarantees when random-observation analyses do not apply.
neurips-2013-matrix-completion-from-any-.tldr: Matrix-completion guarantees for arbitrary observation sets become possible by constructing a distribution over missing entries for evaluating error.

paragraphs: This paper studies whether observations on a graph contain a well-connected region of unusual activation amid Gaussian noise. The challenge is balancing statistical detection power with computational cost. The authors first derive the generalized likelihood ratio test for this problem, but the resulting test is computationally infeasible.

They introduce the Lovasz extended scan statistic, or LESS, as a tractable relaxation. It uses submodularity to approximate the difficult likelihood-ratio calculation. A connection to maximum-a-posteriori inference in Markov random fields then supplies a polynomial-time algorithm, turning the statistical construction into a procedure that can actually be computed efficiently.

The analysis uses electrical network theory to control false positives and establish conditions for risk consistency. The authors further examine torus graphs, k-nearest-neighbor graphs, and epsilon-random graphs, obtaining near-optimal performance relative to known lower bounds on those models. Thus the result combines an efficient relaxation with graph-specific evidence that the computational savings can preserve strong detection performance.
neurips-2013-near-optimal-anomaly-detect.tldr: LESS makes graph anomaly scanning computationally tractable and achieves near-optimal detection guarantees on several specified graph models.

paragraphs: The paper studies convex optimization when an algorithm receives unbiased estimates of gradients rather than exact gradients. It focuses on problems without strong convexity, for which the abstract describes previously known function-value convergence rates of order one over the square root of the number of steps. The authors obtain a faster order-one-over-n rate for two classical supervised-learning problems.

For least-squares regression, averaged stochastic gradient descent achieves this rate with a constant step size. For logistic regression, the authors introduce an algorithm that repeatedly constructs local quadratic approximations to the loss. This second method preserves the running-time complexity of stochastic gradient descent while using the local approximations to support faster convergence.

The theoretical analysis gives finite-sample generalization-error guarantees in expectation, with high-probability guarantees also provided for least squares. Extensive experiments show that the methods often outperform existing approaches. The result demonstrates faster rates in these particular learning settings without asserting the same improvement for every convex problem lacking strong convexity.
neurips-2013-non-strongly-convex-smooth-.tldr: Two stochastic algorithms achieve O(1/n) rates for least-squares and logistic regression without requiring strong convexity.

paragraphs: A deep learning model can contain many weight values, but this paper shows that those values need not all carry independent information. Across several models, the authors find substantial redundancy in the parameterization. Knowing only a few weights associated with a feature can be enough to accurately predict its remaining weights.

The paper takes this observation beyond predicting parameters that have already been learned. The authors train several architectures by learning only a small number of weights and predicting the others. This changes which parameters must be learned directly during training while still supplying values for the rest of the network.

In the strongest reported case, more than 95 percent of the network's weights are predicted without a drop in accuracy. That figure describes the best case, rather than a guarantee for every architecture. The broader finding is that several tested models contain enough parameter redundancy for prediction to replace much of direct weight learning while retaining useful predictive performance.
neurips-2013-predicting-parameters-in-de.tldr: Several deep models can learn only a small share of their weights and predict the rest, exceeding 95 percent predicted weights in the best case without accuracy loss.

paragraphs: Describing a high-dimensional distribution can involve identifying a hierarchy of dense regions rather than just one boundary around typical data. This paper introduces q-OCSVM to estimate such a family of sets efficiently. The method can be used to estimate multiple quantiles of a high-dimensional distribution.

The construction extends the one-class support vector machine by finding several parallel separating hyperplanes in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. These hyperplanes provide the structure for the multiple estimated sets. Instead of treating each set as a separate optimization task, the authors formulate one global convex program that finds all of them together.

The paper shows that this joint program can be solved efficiently and proves the method's correctness. Empirical comparisons also report superiority over existing methods. The contribution is a coordinated way to estimate several levels of a distribution's dense structure, combining a convex formulation with theoretical justification and experimental evidence for the resulting estimates.
neurips-2013-q-ocsvm-a-q-quantile-estima.tldr: q-OCSVM jointly estimates hierarchical dense regions of a high-dimensional distribution through one efficient convex optimization problem.

paragraphs: Sensor selection becomes more selective when only some hidden variables matter for inference and the remaining variables are nuisances. This paper studies that setting for multivariate Gaussian distributions. The goal is to evaluate sensors according to the information relevant to the variables of interest while keeping the calculation efficient in high dimensions.

For vertex pairs connected by a unique graph path, the authors decompose nonlocal mutual information into local information quantities. Those quantities can be computed efficiently from message-passing outputs. The decompositions are incorporated into a greedy sensor selector, and the work required to quantify information can be distributed across network nodes.

Experiments demonstrate the comparative computational efficiency of the resulting selection algorithms. The paper also derives a performance bound that can be calculated online using augmentations of the relevant latent-variable set. When a valid augmentation exists, this bound applies to any distribution with nuisances. That broader bound is conditional, while the principal selection development concerns the Gaussian graphical setting.
neurips-2013-sensor-selection-in-high-di.tldr: Local information decompositions enable efficient sensor selection for Gaussian graphical models with nuisance variables.

paragraphs: Two objects can be similar for different reasons, with each reason depending on a different subset of their features. Similarity Component Analysis models this possibility through hidden components rather than relying on a single metric. Each component independently produces a local similarity value using its own metric.

The model combines those local values through a noisy-OR gate to obtain the overall similarity. The authors develop an expectation-maximization algorithm that fits the probabilistic graphical model from pairwise comparisons annotated with similarity information. This allows the hidden ways of comparing objects to be discovered from the supplied judgments.

On synthetic datasets, SCA recovers the underlying latent components. In multiway classification and link prediction, it achieves significantly higher prediction accuracy than competing methods in the reported experiments. The authors also demonstrate exploratory use: inspecting patterns in the components' local similarity values reveals information about the data. The model therefore supports both prediction and examination of the different relationships underlying observed similarity.
neurips-2013-similarity-component-analys.tldr: Similarity Component Analysis learns hidden, distinct ways objects can be similar and combines them in a probabilistic model.

paragraphs: Sparse additive text models face expensive sums of exponentials, and assuming an identical background across all classes or topics can be restrictive. This paper introduces SAM-LRB, which replaces that shared-background assumption with a low-rank background. It pairs the more flexible model with an estimation procedure designed to reduce computational cost.

A double majorization bound turns the log-likelihood into a quadratic lower-bound approximation without the costly sum-of-exponentials terms. Nuclear-norm and l1-norm regularizers impose low-rank and sparse structure. The resulting optimization takes the same form as a Robust PCA problem, allowing supervised SAM-LRB parameters to be learned using an existing accelerated proximal-gradient algorithm.

The authors also extend the model to unsupervised and multifaceted settings. Experiments on real-world data report effective and efficient learning, with state-of-the-art performance. The approach matters because it addresses model flexibility and optimization together: it relaxes a strong background assumption while converting the fitting problem into a form supported by an established optimization method.
neurips-2013-sparse-additive-text-models.tldr: SAM-LRB adds a low-rank background to sparse text models and enables efficient fitting through a Robust PCA optimization form.

paragraphs: Active learning seeks to learn efficiently by selecting which examples need labels. This paper develops a framework in which algorithms operate through estimated expectations of functions applied to filtered random examples. Building on statistical queries, it makes these statistical operations the basis for designing algorithms that tolerate noisy labels.

The authors show that any efficient active statistical learning algorithm can be converted into an efficient algorithm tolerant to random classification noise and other uncorrelated noise. The resulting complexity has an information-theoretically optimal quadratic dependence on 1/(1−2η), where η is the noise rate. They demonstrate the framework for thresholds, rectangles, and linear separators.

For some of these concept classes, the conversion yields computationally efficient noisy active learners with exponentially improved dependence on target error compared with passive learning. A further conversion produces efficient differentially private active algorithms. The paper reports the first such private algorithms with exponential label savings over passive learning, connecting statistical-query design to both noise tolerance and privacy.
neurips-2013-statistical-active-learning.tldr: A statistical-query framework converts suitable active learners into efficient noise-tolerant and differentially private algorithms.

paragraphs: Sparse data may contain extremely many possible features even though only a few are nonzero in each example. This creates a bottleneck for feature-learning methods that reconstruct an entire input vector during training. Restricted Boltzmann machines face this problem because reconstructing all coordinates can remain expensive even when the observed input is sparse.

The paper adapts an importance-sampling idea previously developed for auto-encoders. Instead of handling every input element during each training example, sampling selects which elements receive computation. The authors introduce stochastic ratio matching for RBMs, retaining the computational advantages and unbiasedness of the importance-sampling scheme.

The authors show that stochastic ratio matching provides a good estimator and report results on the 20 Newsgroups and RCV1 bag-of-words text-classification benchmarks. Their approach beats the state of the art on those two benchmarks while keeping computation linear in the number of nonzero entries. This connects learning quality with a cost measure that reflects actual input sparsity rather than the full feature vocabulary.
neurips-2013-stochastic-ratio-matching-o.tldr: Stochastic ratio matching trains RBMs on sparse inputs with unbiased sampling and computation linear in the number of nonzero features.

paragraphs: Binary hashing represents objects with short sequences of bits and compares those sequences through Hamming distance. The paper considers using this distance to approximate a binary similarity relationship. Its central question is whether both objects in a comparison should be encoded by the same mapping when the original similarity is symmetric.

The authors show that two different encoding maps can produce shorter and more accurate hashes even in that symmetric setting. Instead of comparing f(x) with f(x′), their formulation compares f(x) with g(x′). The change is therefore in the representations assigned to the two positions in a comparison, while the comparison itself still uses Hamming distance.

This finding separates symmetry of the relationship being approximated from symmetry of the encoding procedure. A symmetric target does not rule out benefits from distinct code maps. The stated result establishes that such benefits are possible; it does not claim that every pair of different maps improves hashing or that every symmetric similarity requires asymmetric encodings.
neurips-2013-the-power-of-asymmetry-in-b.tldr: Using different binary encoders for the two objects can yield shorter, more accurate hashes even when the target similarity is symmetric.

paragraphs: Hypergraphs represent higher-order relationships in data, allowing a relationship to involve a group rather than only a pair of objects. This gives them flexibility as learning models. The paper addresses how to build learning methods that use that richer structure directly, rather than relying on a representation that reduces the relationships to ordinary graph connections.

The authors identify two existing approaches: approximating a hypergraph with a graph, and using tensor methods that apply only under special conditions. They propose a new learning framework whose central ingredients are regularization functionals based on total variation on hypergraphs. These functionals bring the hypergraph structure into the formulation of learning itself.

The stated contribution is this direct framework and its family of regularizers. Its significance is that higher-order relationships remain part of the learning formulation, instead of entering only through a graph approximation. The abstract presents a methodological foundation for learning on hypergraphs, with total variation providing the common organizing principle for the proposed regularization functions.
neurips-2013-the-total-variation-on-hype.tldr: A family of hypergraph total-variation regularizers enables learning that directly uses higher-order relationships.

paragraphs: Graph-based Markov decision processes compactly represent sequential decision problems involving many random variables. However, solving them exactly usually requires computation that grows exponentially with the number of variables. This paper introduces a variational framework for planning and derives both exact and approximate algorithms within it.

Its main approximate method is factored variational value iteration. The value function is represented approximately as a product of functions involving local groups of variables. The algorithm then minimizes a Kullback-Leibler divergence using belief propagation. This uses the graph's structure to organize the planning calculation around smaller interacting groups.

The resulting computational complexity is exponential only in graph cluster size, rather than in the full number of variables. Consequently, cluster size remains an important determinant of tractability. Experiments across different models show that the algorithm finds better policies than existing approximation algorithms in those comparisons. The contribution combines a general planning formulation with a specific structural approximation that improves the practical reach of graph-based MDP planning.
neurips-2013-variational-planning-for-gr.tldr: Factored variational value iteration uses graph structure to make approximate MDP planning exponential in cluster size rather than total variable count.
